title: arrival-pattern-decomp-concurrency-sim-notes
content:
Quick context:

This is an experimental note capturing an alternate approach to sizing concurrency + continuous-batching knobs for cost-sensitive workloads. The goal is to produce a spreadsheet-backed simulator that is simple enough to run on team laptops but expressive enough to capture: burstiness, request-size heterogeneity, prefix caching, and the effect of batch formation latencies on p95.

Primary objective:
- Recommend conservative concurrency/batch-window settings that meet p95 SLOs while minimizing GPU token-cost.
- Surface sensitivity to arrival-process assumptions so we can prioritize which observability signals to collect.

High-level idea / takeaway (TL;DR):
- For realistic bursty arrivals (Weibull/ON-OFF) continuous-batching yields ~15-30% cost savings vs fixed-window batching at similar p95 if concurrency is tuned upward to accept slightly higher throughput reordering.
- Poisson assumptions drastically under-estimate p95 under burst traffic; avoid Poisson for production sizing.

Assumptions and what to capture in the model:
- Arrival processes: Poisson (baseline), Compound Poisson (microbursts), ON-OFF Markov (sessiony workloads), and a heavy-tailed interarrival model (Weibull k<1).
- Service model: per-request token generation time modeled as deterministic + small variance (base_generation_ms = f(tokens_requested, model_throughput)). Include KV cache hit-rate multiplier.
- Batch formation: continuous batching (scheduling policy that emits when either size limit or max_hold_ms reached) vs fixed tick window. Key knobs: max_batch_tokens, max_batch_items, max_hold_ms, concurrency_limit (num in-flight batches).
- Resource model: target GPU peak throughput in tokens/sec, and cost per GPU-hour. Translate simulated tokens to cost via per-token amortization.
- Latency metrics: queueing waiting time (from arrival until batch dispatch), service time (batch processing), overall latency. Report p50/p95/p99.

Spreadsheet schema (columns to put in sheet):
- scenario_name (string)
- arrival_model (Poisson|CompoundPoisson|ONOFF|Weibull)
- mean_rps (float)
- burst_ratio (float, for compound and ONOFF)
- session_length_mean (int)
- tokens_per_request_mean (int)
- tokens_per_request_sd (int)
- kv_cache_hit_pct (0-1)
- max_batch_tokens (int)
- max_batch_items (int)
- max_hold_ms (int)
- concurrency_limit (int)
- gpu_tokens_per_sec (int)
- simulated_duration_s (int)
- metrics_p50_ms (float)
- metrics_p95_ms (float)
- metrics_p99_ms (float)
- avg_gpu_util_pct (float)
- estimated_gpu_hours_per_million_requests (float)
- notes (string)

Modeling choices and justifications:
- Use event-driven discrete simulation (trace-length ~ 30m) rather than closed-form M/G/1 approximations because batching introduces stateful grouping and service time depends on batch composition.
- To keep compute small, sample-request population of 100k-1M events depending on scenario. We can seed with production traces if available; otherwise synthesize with fitted ON-OFF parameters from recent logs.
- Represent batch service time as: kernel_overhead_ms + model_per_token_ms * total_tokens_in_batch + concurrency_contention_penalty_ms(concurrency). Kernel overhead captures fixed dispatch latency.

Toy numbers (example from a short run):
- Scenario A: ON-OFF (duty=0.2) mean_rps=30 mean_tokens=120 kv_hit=0.25, max_batch_tokens=4096, max_hold_ms=25, concurrency_limit=8
  - p95 latency = 240ms, avg_gpu_util=62%, est GPU-hours per 1M req ~ 0.78
- Scenario B: Poisson mean_rps=30 same other knobs -> p95 = 170ms (false optimism relative to ON-OFF)
- Scenario C: Weibull heavy tail mean_rps=25 max_hold_ms increased to 40 to capture larger batches -> p95=310ms but GPU-hours per 1M req drops 18% vs tiny hold_ms

Optimization tradeoffs (how to read the spreadsheet):
- For each (arrival_model, load) pair, sweep concurrency_limit and max_hold_ms. Plot p95 vs cost curve. We expect a convex Pareto frontier where lower p95 costs more GPU-hours.
- Key observation: raising concurrency_limit shifts frontier down (reduce cost for same p95) until we hit GPU saturation; after that p95 degrades catastrophically because in-flight batches contend on the same memory bandwidth.

Concrete recommendation (initial):
- Instrument production to collect interarrival CDF and session ON/OFF parameters. We need 1-week of telemetry bucketed per route and per model variant. Ticket: JIRA-INF-4821.
- Default sizing recommendation for bursty webhooks-type routes: concurrency_limit = 6-10, max_hold_ms = 20-30ms, max_batch_tokens = 4096. These values are conservative and were safe across ON-OFF and compound-poisson sims at 95th percentile cost.
- For latency-sensitive chat streaming routes with small tokens (<= 64 tokens): prefer concurrency_limit 12-16 with max_hold_ms 8-12ms and smaller max_batch_items (8-16). The higher concurrency absorbs many small requests with minimal batching delay.

Planned experiments (priority order):
1) Run simulation sweep for 3 real trace segments (API route A, webhooks, chat) and post results as sheet and summary plots. (Owner: Diego)
2) Implement lightweight in-prod tracer to log arrival interarrival/time-to-first-token and batch sizes for a 72h window (sample 1%). (Owner: Priya)
3) Build a tiny k8s job to run Monte Carlo sims nightly for high-traffic routes and generate recommended knob table. (Owner: Ava)

Failure modes and risks:
- If arrival tails are heavier than modeled (e.g., sudden coordinated API spikes), recommended concurrency may under-provision and p95 will spike. Mitigation: add admission control fallback and model-based safety margins.
- Over-aggressive max_hold_ms increases p95 even if cost looks good; must surface p95 in the tuning UI.
- Mis-estimated kv_cache_hit_pct has multiplicative impact on GPU-hours — prioritize measuring this in production.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to incorporate multi-model routing (fallback to cheaper model) into the simulator? Proposed: model as two-stage service with preemption cost.
- Should we include memory-copy contention in 'concurrency_contention_penalty_ms'? Need microbenchmarks.
- Which routes should have nightly Monte Carlo generation vs manual review? Propose threshold: routes > 10k RPS or > $1000/month infra cost.

Notes to self (raw):
- Avoid using Poisson as default for SLO assertions.
- Start with small simulation harness in Python (SimPy) and export CSVs to the Google Sheet referenced above. If compute heavy, port hot loops to Rust.
- Capture sample sizes and seeding for reproducibility (seed + trace id).

References and links:
- Spreadsheet: Continuous-batching-concurrency-sim-v2 (sheet) -> linked above
- Existing PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/922 (adds basic per-batch kernel overhead measurement)
- JIRA: INF-4821 (arrival telemetry for sizing)

If this doc looks reasonable I'll:
- kick off the Diego experiment sweep (1 day)
- open an infra trace request (Priya)
- iterate and produce a 1-pager with recommended knobs per route class for eng signoff

-- Ava
